chunks.text: Known in India as bakul and in English as Spanish cherry, bullet wood or medlar, Mimusops elengi is a medium-sized evergreen tree of the Sapotaceae family native to coastal South and Southeast Asia and northern Australia, typically standing some 9 to 18 metres tall with glossy dark-green oval leaves and intensely fragrant, hairy cream-coloured flowers that bloom around April; its fleshy fruit, ripening between June and October from yellow through to a deeper reddish-brown, is edible around a single large hard-coated seed. Its timber is notably dense and strong, with a rich deep-red heartwood that takes a fine polish, historically valued as a genuinely premium hardwood rather than an ordinary building timber. In Thailand, the sun-dried flowers are steeped to make floral infusions and are sometimes added to green tea for their scent, and the flowers more broadly are noted as a material used in natural perfumery, consistent with their famously long-lasting fragrance even after drying — a property that underlies the tree's enduring role across India in flower garlands offered at temples and worn by women, since, unlike many fresh blooms, bakul flowers keep their scent well after being strung and even after they have dried out completely. The species carries official symbolic status outside India too: its flower is the provincial emblem of Yala Province in Thailand and the city flower of Ampang Jaya in Malaysia. It was formally described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753 and is currently assessed as Least Concern by the IUCN.

chunks.source: Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry (2012) — ethnobotanical, phytochemical and pharmacological review of Mimusops elengi
chunks.text: This peer-reviewed pharmacognosy review consolidates the scientific literature on bakul's traditional and investigated medicinal properties, and is useful precisely because it separates long-standing folk use from what has actually been tested in a laboratory. Traditionally, Ayurvedic and other Indian folk medical systems use the bark, fruit and seeds of the tree, generally describing their action as astringent, tonic and fever-reducing. Chemically, the review reports that the bark contains tannins and a small amount of natural rubber-like caoutchouc along with wax and starch, the flowers yield a volatile aromatic oil consistent with their use in perfumery, and the seeds contain a fixed fatty oil. On the pharmacological side, the review summarises a substantial list of properties that have been examined in preclinical, laboratory and animal studies — including pain-relieving, antimicrobial, lipid-lowering, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, fever-reducing, cytotoxic and blood-pressure-lowering activity, along with effects on gastric ulceration and gum health. It is important to be clear about what this does and does not establish: these are preclinical findings only, not confirmed results from human clinical trials, so while they suggest Mimusops elengi is phytochemically active and a reasonable candidate for further pharmaceutical research, none of this amounts to proven, clinically validated therapeutic efficacy or safety in people.
